headline_marked: [[Gmail changes]] star and important markers from yellow to blue for accessibility
headline: Gmail changes star and important markers from yellow to blue for accessibility
summary: Google's move to blue indicators aims to improve readability and inclusivity, but some users are unhappy with the aesthetic shift.
details: Gmail has begun rolling out a change that replaces the familiar yellow stars and "Important" message markers with a new blue hue. This alteration has sparked discussion among users, with some expressing frustration over the aesthetic shift.

Google states the change is a deliberate move to enhance accessibility, aligning with modern standards. The company explained that the blue color offers better contrast against white backgrounds, meeting Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) recommendations.

While yellow can struggle to meet WCAG contrast ratios on white backgrounds, a bright blue easily achieves the required contrast. This ensures inboxes are clearer and easier to read for a wider range of users, including those with visual impairments.

Despite the accessibility benefits, some users find the blue markers blend too closely with Gmail's existing color scheme, potentially making them harder to distinguish cognitively. However, Google maintains that the change does not violate accessibility guidelines.

For users who preferred the original yellow stars, there is a setting to revert this specific change. By navigating to Settings > See all settings > General > Stars, users can re-select yellow. This change will apply to future messages.

The "Important" marker color, however, cannot be changed back. Users who dislike the blue "Important" marker can opt to disable importance markers entirely by going to Settings > See all settings > Inbox > Importance markers and selecting 'No markers'.

headline_marked: Google [[sends AI satellite]] into space with Tensor Processing Units
headline: Google sends AI satellite into space with Tensor Processing Units
summary: Google's Project Suncatcher aims to test AI hardware in orbit, with plans for a constellation of chip-equipped satellites.
details: Google is launching a satellite equipped with its Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) on October 1st aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket. This mission is part of the experimental Project Suncatcher, which aims to eventually place AI data centers into orbit.

The primary goal is to assess how Google's TPUs perform under the extreme conditions of space, including radiation and thermal variations, and the physical stresses of spaceflight. While ground testing showed resilience, Google states that 'some things can only be tested in space.'

The satellite will harness solar power in low Earth orbit. A key test will involve a new cooling system designed for the chips, which will require them to be turned off for approximately 15 minutes every hour to prevent overheating.

This initiative is part of a broader vision, shared by figures like Elon Musk and Jeff Bezos, to explore space as a viable location for scalable AI compute. Google plans to launch two more satellites next year to further this objective.

Project Suncatcher's senior director of product management, Travis Beals, emphasized that this is a methodical engineering process. The initial launch is crucial for identifying what works, potential failure points, and gathering data to inform future missions.
